In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#460 out of 612)... it's time for Company of Heroes: Opposing Fronts.

Company of Heroes is, without question or doubt, easily the definitive WWII-era real-time tactical strategy game. Nothing else on the market even comes close—except for its own expansions. Enter Opposing Fronts. The big addition of Opposing Fronts is the two new campaigns, which add a good dozen or so hours of new content as well as two new playable "factions" (is that an odd word to use in this context, or is that just me?) -- the British 2nd Army and the German Panzer Elite. But perhaps the most compelling addition, I think, is the new set of semi-randomized weather affects, which make the game a bit more interesting (and unpredictable) to play while also making for much more dramatic visuals.

If the Company of Heroes game fails in any one respect, it's probably that it over-romanticizes the second World War. If you're looking for nuanced storytelling or more realistic tactics (supply lines aren't much of an issue here) you're not going to find it: this is still [i]Saving Private Ryan[/i]: the game. Which is another way of saying no camps, no cavalry, just mud, blood and Hollywood high drama. Whether or not this is a good thing, a bad thing, or reason to avoid the game entirely is up to the person, obviously, my point here is only that Opposing Fronts retains the same themes and tones of the original game, so don't go into it expecting anything wildly different. It is, for better or worse, more of the same.

Company of Heroes is an older games, but even despite its age it stands out as one of the finest tactical strategy games out there, and it's easy to see why. Opposing Fronts takes everything about the original game that was great, building upon it to create the definitive WWII game.

Company of Heroes: Opposing Fronts builds on the foundations of the original game while confidently standing as its own complete experience, offering two full-length campaigns and new factions that dramatically shift how battles unfold. Rather than feeling like a minor add-on, it expands the scope of the Company of Heroes formula by placing players in the shoes of armies rarely given center stage in WWII RTS games. The British 2nd Army’s push through Caen and the German Panzer Elite’s desperate resistance during Operation Market Garden present contrasting tones, pacing, and tactical demands. These two perspectives allow the expansion to feel broader and more varied, presenting the war as a series of complex, evolving struggles rather than a simple sequence of American-led victories. Both campaigns are cinematic, tightly directed, and filled with the environmental destruction and battlefield chaos that defined the original game while offering new tactical challenges unique to each faction.

The British campaign highlights slow, methodical progress anchored in defensive superiority. Their forces rely on emplacements, trenches, officer support, and heavy artillery to establish a creeping frontline. This approach rewards players who manage territory carefully, choosing when to dig in and when to push forward. Every inch of ground matters, and the British army’s reliance on positioning and entrenchment creates battles that feel tense and deliberate. In contrast, the Panzer Elite demands constant motion. Their focus on fast vehicles, lightweight armor, and versatile half-tracks shifts the pace toward hit-and-run attacks, flanking maneuvers, and opportunistic strikes. Playing as the Panzer Elite forces you to always think ahead, repositioning before the enemy reacts, and taking advantage of mobility to compensate for fragility. This difference in faction rhythm provides a refreshing contrast, inviting players to rethink their usual strategic habits.

One of the expansion’s strongest qualities is its use of the Essence Engine, which still stands out for how dynamically it simulates destruction. Buildings crumble under repeated shelling, roads turn into fractured debris fields, and sightlines shift as cover is destroyed or created. The addition of new weather effects, better lighting, and improved terrain detail gives missions a stronger sense of place. Even though weather does not drastically alter gameplay, it deepens immersion and helps maintain variety across the campaigns. The battlefield feels alive, reactive, and unpredictable, which enriches both single-player and multiplayer matches. Watching a tank smash through a farmhouse or a barrage reduce a fortified position to rubble remains as satisfying now as it was at release.

Multiplayer remains one of Opposing Fronts’ enduring strengths. Adding the British and Panzer Elite to the roster opens up new strategic pairings and matchups. British defensive lines combined with American armor create potent Allied synergies, while Panzer Elite mobility can complement the Wehrmacht’s heavier, more traditional infantry and tank approaches. Matches become a dance of territory control, unit composition, and timing. The core Company of Heroes design—capturing resource sectors, protecting your supply lines, and using terrain properly—remains untouched, but the addition of two radically different factions brings new strategic layers. The expansion preserves the tight balance that made the original competitive scene so respected, offering players more ways to express their tactical style.

Opposing Fronts does have occasional weaknesses. The structure of many missions remains rooted in familiar patterns such as holding a position under pressure or pushing through fortified choke points. While the campaigns are engaging, players may notice repetition in mission design or map usage. Newcomers might also find the British and Panzer Elite more complex than the original factions due to their reliance on nuanced mechanics like emplacements, officer buffs, vehicle-centric squads, or doctrine abilities that significantly alter how they function. Some graphical improvements, such as weather cycles, serve more as visual flair than meaningful tactical tools. These issues, however, do not undermine the overall strength and variety the expansion brings.

Despite these flaws, Company of Heroes: Opposing Fronts succeeds as both an accessible standalone entry and a meaningful expansion for veterans. It expands the Company of Heroes universe with well-designed factions, memorable campaigns, and atmospheric battles that maintain the tension and tactical weight of the original. It respects what made Company of Heroes influential while confidently adding its own innovations. Even years after its release, Opposing Fronts remains a strong example of how to extend an RTS without losing focus or diluting what made the base game great. For strategy fans, it stands as a richly crafted portrayal of WWII combat, blending cinematic presentation with deep tactical decision-making in a way few games have matched.

[h1]Company of Heroes: Opposing Fronts[/h1]
[h3]Amazing DLC with very Solid Content[/h3]
[h3]Really worth getting with the full game bundle[/h3]

Opposing Fronts is the first DLC for the game and the one that added the most content out of the two expansions released for the first installment. In many ways, it is an excellent expansion that added great replayability value to the game at the time by introducing new armies, units, and maps. 

This expansion introduced the Panzer Elite and the British Commonwealth, two unique factions with their own strengths and weaknesses that added more variety to the game. Although to be honest, the British Commonwealth feels like an underdeveloped faction, with rough game mechanics and an unusually slow gameplay style. Unlike the British, the Panzer Elite became one of the strongest factions in the game, especially in multiplayer thanks to its fast and aggressive playstyle. 

The campaigns introduced in this expansion are equally enjoyable and challenging.The difficulty is well balanced during the first missions, where the core mechanics of each faction are introduced. However, the later ones can become extremely difficult, requiring us to destroy seemingly endless waves of armored vehicles and heavy infantry. On the other hand, the level design is varied, with each scenario having unique objectives and different ways to complete them. Both campaigns have a reasonable length, especially considering that they are additional content for the base game.

From a historical perspective, this expansion takes a considerable amount of creative liberties and condenses many ot the events of the operations it portrays, simplifying large and complex battles into smaller playable scenarios. This is understandable to some extent, given that it is an expansion rather than another full game. However, the way these battles are presented feels somewhat linear and provides little sense of how much time passes between events.

[h3]Liberation of Caen[/h3]
As an introductory campaign for the British Commonwealth, it is quite comprehensive, showcasing both the basic and more advanced mechanics of the faction. It also features a good variety of missions, including sabotage operations, seek-and-destroy sections, and defensive scenarios. However, these latter missions suffer from some gameplay balance issues, even on the intermediate difficulties. It is impressive how many enemies these scenarios throw at you while providing such a limited resource income to defend key points on the map. Overall, it is a fairly entertaining campaign, but it has certain issues that prevent it from being fully enjoyable. 

[h3]Operation Market Garden[/h3]
Compared to the British campaign, it covers fewer of the Panzer Elite's mechanics and war doctrines, making it less of an introductory campaign and more of a collection of straightforward, combat-focused missions. The main issue with this campaign is that several missions reuse the same scenarios, only under different weather conditions or at night, with objectives focused on defending strategic points. For the previous reason, this campaign can feel somewhat repetitive.

Operation Market Garden is an enjoyable campaign that makes some use of the Panzer Elite's unique mechanics, although it does not explore the faction as thoroughly as it could. Regarding this, the Panzer Elite, in particular, does not represent any specific Wehrmacht division or regiment, but rather combines different German units under a single faction built around a fast and highly mechanized playstyle.

Greetings as always.  Today we will be looking at “Opposing Fronts” the first of two DLC expansions for Company of Heroes.  COH is easily one of the best of the post C&C world of the RTS genre and only now am I just getting around to this expansion; with that said I’m very interested in seeing if this game still holds up.  Let’s discuss.

Fish and Chips:  As always with DLC I won’t be going over the core mechanics and assume you already have the base game.  Opposing Fronts brings two new factions (British and Panzer Elite) both have more of a mobile aesthetic overall (even with their defensive formations).  The British base elements can be packed up and moved at will and have command units that give bonuses to nearby infantry / vehicles.  The Panzer Elite oddly (being a non-history buff) don’t have a lot of tanks but focus on a core infantry that is heavily customizable and expandable as they advance.  They do also have a few tanks towards the end game but definitely not what I would expect from the ‘Panzer’ focus but have some formations that do open up some very nasty armor.  Both factions, at the core, seem to struggle a bit against armor but do have their ways of dealing with them.  In addition to the factions you get two well done campaigns, arguably more content then the core game.   These campaigns are well done and had stories that were easy to follow and at least felt historically accurate.

Sauerkraut:  The only real issues I had with this game is that the AI does not seem to understand how to play with the British, half of the skirmishes I played against them they wouldn’t really do anything.  There were some pathing issues in the new maps (both campaign and skirmish) but nothing that completely broke down the game.  The persistent map feature (allowing missions to carry over to the next with map layout and units) tended to be a bit annoying as the unit need shifted (for example a mission needing heavy infantry to one that focused on tanks).

Overall the DLC is well worth the money and does go on sale fairly often.  I’d happily pay retail for the content but if you wait you can save a bit of money.  The game itself still holds up very well to this day, graphics and all and still feel like a revolutionary game in the RTS genre.  Enjoy!

[h1]Short review[/h1]

Longer, more beautiful, stronger, this could be the motto of Opposing Fronts. The original game was already excellent, this stand-alone is even better since it takes up the basics while enriching them with new possibilities. The addition of a second campaign corrects the main complaint against Company of Heroes and extends the lifespan. In short, no need to procrastinate any longer, after this praise it is clear that this game was a reference for other strategy games in it's time.

[h1]Long review[/h1]

The developers of Relic made the choice for this release to be a standalone and not an extension, the game seeks above all to conquer newcomers, even if it is obviously also addressed to the old men of the first episode in search of new challenges. For the former, let's recall the basics of the gameplay of Company of Heroes. The battles are centered around the capture of strategic points scattered around the map, reminiscent of previous productions by the Canadian studio such as Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War. Depending on their nature, these points yield three types of resources: ammunition, fuel and manpower. Once under the player's control, they give you these resources regularly as long as they are located in a territory connected to the Headquarters. No need for a harvest phase, therefore, or construction of expensive buildings like in other such titles, for that matter. The only possible constructions are a few defensive works, such as sites for mortars, machine guns or howitzers. Partly freed from constraints linked to the economy and the development of a base, the player can therefore concentrate on the management of his troops, towards which the game is resolutely turned.

And we will have to pamper them, these troops. Each of your units is valuable, since over the course of the battles they gain experience, which is used to acquire new abilities. Better to try to preserve your men rather than send them to die without having to replace them with newbies. To do this, you have to use the terrain as much as possible to take cover. Anything can serve as a shelter, but a low wall for example will offer much better protection. Likewise, soldiers can enter buildings to be less exposed. However, keep in mind that everything is destructible, so a tank will easily dislodge them. Tanks, in fact, should preferably be attacked from behind, where their armor is weaker. In short, blindly rushing will never be the winning strategy, each assault requires proper planning, which is not an easy task in the urgency of some situations. All these aspects already present in Company of Heroes are of course found in Opposing Fronts. On this side, the veterans of the first opus will not be disoriented. So let's now see what are the novelties brought by this standalone.

Two new armies are emerging: the British and the German Panzer Elite armored division. Let's start by reviewing the British Army troops. First of all, their base is mobile. It consists of a truck that we can deploy wherever we want, then fold up to move it to another point of the map where it is more needed. Practical. Also, in the vehicles section, we obviously find tank models specific to this nation, such as the Tetrarch or the Cromwell. But my favorite is still the huge Churchill. The tank, not the Prime Minister man. It is available in several versions modified by the Royal Engineers, known historically as Hobart's Funnies. Specialists will therefore appreciate the presence of the AVRE, equipped with a powerful mortar, or the Crocodile and its flamethrower which is very practical when you have to deal with infantry. At the infantry level, officers (lieutenants and captains) can be attached to your sections of riflemen to give them bonuses. Soldiers can dig trenches to establish a line of defense. Gliders are also available to quickly deploy commandos or armor on the battlefield, thus creating advanced spawn points. Finally, the command point system is still present and will allow the leader of the British Army to call for help. For example, a Canadian artillery support, such as the 'rolling barrage', terribly effective against enemy troops.

The British campaign takes place in Normandy, and you will experience many historical events such as the famous capture of Hill 112, which we will then have to desperately defend during a counter-attack a few missions further away. All of this will take us until the liberation of the city of Caen. The German campaign, meanwhile, puts you at the head of the Panzer Elite Armored Division in the massive Airborne Operation Market Garden. For those who have skipped their history lessons, a little reminder: this allied operation was intended to bypass the Siegfried line via the Netherlands. It ended in a terrible failure. At the head of the German forces, your goal will therefore be to reproduce history by pushing back this offensive. To help you many new units are available. One of the most useful is undoubtedly the halftrack. With this vehicle the player has a quick and efficient portable mortar that can pound enemy positions while remaining relatively behind.  Panzergrenadiers are also very practical with their heavy armament. They constitute shock infantry. I'm not going to make an exhaustive list of the units brought by Opposing Fronts because there would still be a lot to detail, but they are numerous and varied enough to renew the interest of Company of Heroes and to give birth to new tactics. In any case for the first time that they are playable in a campaign, the Germans do not disappoint as the Panzer Elite forces are really pleasant to handle.

With these two new solo campaigns, this standalone already sets the bar very high in terms of gameplay and lifespan, but the technique is no exception. The game is beautiful, like the original, maybe even a little more thanks to new effects, especially for the weather. However, keep in mind that this game is old, it was beautiful when it released. This game is a great show, a bit like a Call of Duty but seen from above: grenades and shells explode while houses crumble under a rain of iron and fire, all supported by incredibly realistic sound effects and thunderous music. I think I can stop the list of superlatives there, you will understand that the production from Relic was once again grandiose, which after all is not surprising from the creators of Homeworld. I'm just able to find a little flaw: the zoom out isn't enough, we're still a bit too close to the action for my taste. A wider view of the field would have been appreciated. There is the cons. But it's not this kind of trifle that will stop Company Of Heroes: Opposing Fronts from rising to the top of the pantheon of real-time strategy.

[h1]TL:DR? See Conclusion[/h1]

[h1]INTRODUCTION:[/h1]
Company of Heroes: Opposing Fronts is a real-time strategy game developed by Relic Entertainment and published by THQ (RIP). This game serves as the first official expansion pack to the series which adds two new factions, new units, a German (Panzer Elite) and British campaigns along with new multiplayer maps.

The expansion pack 'Opposing Fronts' added 2 new campaigns for the new factions of Great Britain who's plot revolves around the British Royal Army's operation to retake and secure the city of Caen in northern France. On the other-hand, the new Axis campaign featured the Panzer Elite faction in their mission to foil an Allied Operation called 'Market Garden'.

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
+ Improved special effects
+ New Factions
+ German and British Campaigns
+ New Units are fun to play with
+ Standalone Expansion but...(See CON #3)
+ Allows players with the expansion to play with players without the expansions and vice versa

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
- Balance issues
- AI is somehow worse than the original
- Does not include the original armies unless you have the original game
- Campaign has some dull moments
- Inconsistent sound / voice levels for some of the units

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
GOOD EXPANSION but could have used a little more polish. Opposing Fronts is a great expansion that adds a lot of replayability to the original game by adding new factions; new units; new Campaign and a ton of improvements that increases the authentic feel and immersion of the game.

MUST BUY for RTS and World War 2 fans whether at full price or on sale. Although, I highly advice the [b]'Complete Pack'[/b] (which includes the original game and the 2 expansions) to have the full experience.

[h1][b][u]GAMEPLAY[/u]: 8.5/10[/b][/h1]

Mostly classic RTS game mechanics, no major flaws to point out. You have good controls over your units, and you better be ! Because Company of hero puts the emphasis on unit veterancy, so forget sending troops to the meat grinder. You have to keep track of every unit and keep them alive at all cost in order to accumulate veterancy. COH is a rigorous RTS that rewards your intelligence and your skills.

[h1][b][u]LEVEL DESIGN[/u]: 9/10[/b][/h1]
 
Maps are great, many building to take advantages of (a church to put your sniper, a well placed house to put your mg etc...) same goes for a nicely placed hill to line up your mortars. Fight for map control, blow up briges to block routes and funnel the enemy, build defences etc.... This game's level design combined its gameplay truelly allows the strategy god inside of you to shine !

[h1][b][u]VISUAL & ART[/u]: 8/10[/b][/h1]

The Revolutionary RTS.

Gone is the simple spam and zerg tactics of the classic style, gone is the throwaway hordes of troops.
Now each man, each vehicle, and where you place them mattered. The environment providing cover, concealment, and chokepoints. Less emphasis on refining your build queue and your most efficient productions. More emphasis on tactical placement, securing vital territory, and improvising on the fly.

The Gold Standard every RTS should aspire to.

Opposing Fronts is the first expansion to Company of Heroes, and is by far the single most important of the pieces to pick up. OF adds the British and the Panzer Elite factions into the game. Britian is my personal favorite faction, and it favors strong, fortified defence and a generalized infantry-centric army that can deal with any threats, athough not reallty specializing in any field. Meanwhile, the Panzer Elite (Poorly named as they have only one actual tank) focuses on an extremely offensive and mobile army in which highly specailized vechicles perform a narrow role, and thus every unit serves a spefific purpose. Both factions are extremly unique, and do not feel like retooled American/Wehrmacht. OF also adds two new campaigns for the two new factions. In all, if you loved CoH, you will adore the hell out of this expansion.

NOTE: Getting this expansion only, without the base or Tales of Valor, means that you will only be able to play as the British or Panzer Elite.

By far my favorite RTS game EVER! It's like playing a game of Rock, Paper, Scissors, except your rock, paper, or scissors are upgradeable so as not to be completely countered by something else. For example, infantry can possess various upgrades purchased for them in order to sustain their survivability against say a tank, and the squad intelligence level is simply astounding. Individual squad members will try to seek out the best cover possible on their own, yet always staying within a certain radius of the rest of the squad. While tank battles are generally favorable towards German armor (historically accurate), Company of Heroes makes sure that one is never totally outmatched by offering various counter techniques or upgrades. To take the battles online is even more amusing, with a still-active online community. 

CoH is hard to compare to other titles, such as the Starcraft/Warcraft series, Sins of a Solar Empire, Rise of Nations, etc due to its unique style of gameplay. It is MUCH slower in pace when put next to other RTS games, which in my opinion, is what makes it amazing. Battles take a while, and you don't have to be worried about throwing the game if you lose the first few large-scale fights.

The game looks beautiful, plays wonderfully, and is among one of the best RTS games to have reached the shelves. If you're still not convinced, check out the demo (which gives you a good preview of how the game looks and feels).
